deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 61 (numbered '61' at top right, with a pencil '31' in the right margin) is a page of German prose notes on ancient Greek history, written in the style of a school or lecture notebook. It continues directly from folio 60 (Sparta and the Messenian Wars) and carries on into folio 62 (Athenian kings and archons, Draco, Solon). The hand and content look like student history notes and may not be Gauss's own writing. There is nothing to reconstruct in a mathematical sense.

The content runs as follows:

(1) End of the Second Messenian War. The Messenians formed an alliance with the Arcadians, but the Arcadian king abandoned them and they were defeated. The Spartans had a bard, Tyrtaeus, who roused them to warlike deeds. The war was decided at the stronghold of Eira. Sparta subjugated the whole country and the Messenians were reduced to serfs (helots). This lasted until Epaminondas made Messenia an independent state again.

(2) Section 'B. Geschichte von Athen' (History of Athens). The Athenian state covered only Attica, a small mountainous land with the streams Ilissus and Cephisus. Cephisus is added in the margin and keyed with a '+'. The capital Athen lay on these streams, and the most famous mountain is Hymettus. Pelasgians with their own kings lived there originally. Egyptian colonists came early under Cecrops (1550). Cecrops divided the land into 4 districts, and Attica then had 20,000 inhabitants. After him came Erechtheus, Pandion and Aegeus; under Aegeus the land became tributary to the king of Crete. Theseus, who came to power in 1232, made it independent again. He is said to have built (unified) the city, introduced a constitution, and divided the people into three classes: nobles, farmers and tradesmen. The page breaks off at 'During the Trojan War there reigned…', and the next page continues with 'Menestheus'.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.

Historically, the dates (Cecrops 1550, Theseus 1232) and the Egyptian origin of Cecrops reflect 18th–19th-century chronological conventions, not modern scholarship. They are standard for the period, not slips.
The list of kings is written with corrections: Pandion is struck and rewritten below, and 'Egeus Egas' is corrected to 'Aegeus'. The intended sequence is Erechtheus, Pandion, Aegeus.

results.what: Narrative notes on the end of the Second Messenian War and the early (mythical) history of Athens (Cecrops to Theseus)
results.modern_name: Not mathematics: ancient Greek history lecture notes
results.usually_credited_to: Standard textbook material of the period (e.g. Heeren-style ancient history courses)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains only routine school or lecture notes on Greek history, possibly not even in Gauss's hand. It has no mathematical content of any kind.
transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'einen Lorden Tyrtäus' should almost certainly read 'einen Barden Tyrtäus' (Tyrtaeus the bard/poet).
Line 4: the inserted word read as 'wassige' is doubtful; context suggests 'Einnahme' (capture). 'Platzes' is doubtful too; it may be 'Fleckens' or 'Festung' Eira.
Lines 7–8: the reading is better as 'bis auf die Zeiten des Epaminondas, der Messenien wieder zu einem eignen Staat machte'. 'daß' and 'gemacht wurde' are struck; 'einzig' is likely 'eignen'.
Ilissus line: the marginal '+ Cephisus' is keyed to the '+' after 'Ilissus'. The reading is 'mit den Flüßchen Ilissus und Cephisus, an denen die Hauptstadt Athen lag'.
'kamen Ägyptische Colonisten 1550 Cecrops' is probably 'kamen Ägyptische Colonisten unter Cecrops 1550'.
King list: 'Nach ihm sind Erechtheus, Pandion und Aegeus'. The struck 'Pandion' is rewritten on the line below; 'Egeus Egas' is struck and replaced by 'Aegeus'.
The pencil '31' in the right margin and the folio number '61' at top right are not part of the text.
